about: The acclamation joins the cry of the seraphim in Isaiah's vision (Is 6:3) to the words of the crowd welcoming Christ into Jerusalem (Mt 21:9). The threefold Sanctus praises the Lord God of hosts, whose glory fills heaven and earth. The Benedictus blesses Him who comes in the name of the Lord.

s01.narrative: The Preface comes to its end. The priest joins his hands before his breast, bows, and says the Sanctus in a moderate voice while the server rings the bell. At the words “Benedíctus qui venit in nómine Dómini” he straightens up and signs himself with the cross from forehead to breast. The Canon begins immediately after, said silently.

s02.translation: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.

s03.translation: Heaven and earth are full of Your glory.

s05.translation: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.

w001.function: “Sanctus”, repeated three times, refers to “Dóminus” (w004) and is therefore nominative masculine. The copula “est” is understood.

w006.function: The form carries no case ending — the Hebrew word entered Latin without inflection. In this title it does a genitive's work: the Lord God of hosts.

w007.function: Nominative masculine plural, agreeing with “cæli” (w009), the first of the two subjects.

w012.function: Ablative governed by “Pleni” (w007). English marks the relation with “of”: “full of glory”.

w017.function: A predicate with an implied “est”. Its subject is the relative clause beginning with “qui” (w018).

w018.function: A relative pronoun beginning a clause with the sense “he who comes”.

w019.function: Present tense. The perfect “vēnit” has the same spelling but a different first-vowel quantity.

w021.function: Ablative after “in” (w020) in the fixed phrase “in nómine Dómini”: “in the name of the Lord”.
